newsitem.title: GERMANY: German public, private banks to meet in subsidy row.
newsitem.headline: German public, private banks to meet in subsidy row.

text.p: Germany's private and public banks meet this week to tackle a dispute over alleged subsidies which could, if it festers much longer, spark a full European Union probe into how the public banks get their capital.

The heads of the private and public banking associations, Karl-Heinz Wessel and Friedel Neuber respectively, as well as German government representatives will meet EU Competition Commissioner Karel van Miert for talks in Brussels on Friday.

The dispute centres on a complaint filed in 1994 by the Federal Association of German Banks, which represents private sector banks, that 11 billion marks ($6.9 billion) of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.
If it is not resolved, the EU is expected to start an investigation into state guarantees available to public banks which have enabled them to gain top credit ratings.

The regional banks, or Landesbanken, are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.

In 1990 the federal states started integrating their regional housing development agencies into the regional banks to beef up the banks' weak equity capital before tougher EU rules on capital adequacy came into force in 1993.
In one case WestLB, the biggest regional bank, received four billion marks in fresh equity capital by integrating North Rhine-Westphalia's housing development agency in 1992.

The private banks see this as distorting competition because it enabled the regional banks to obtain capital at a far lower price than would be charged for funds in the private sector. The regional banks see no such distortion.
The two sides on Tuesday appeared no nearer to a compromise than when the last round of talks failed late last year.

"I think we've proposed everything that could be done from the point of view of the public banks and now the question is if the private banks accept it," Henning Schoppmann, spokesman for the Association of Public Banks, told Reuters.

Schoppmann said WestLB already paid an interest rate of 0.6 percent for the capital. It was also prepared to pay the state all earnings gains resulting from the capital injection if the bank is ever privatised.
Thomas Schlueter, spokesman for the Federal Association of German Banks said an interest rate of 0.6 percent was well below interest rates charged for capital in the private sector.
"We are ready to compromise but it's clear that subsidies have been paid and the issue now is to find an appropriate rate of interest for the housing agency funds," Schlueter said.
"The regional banks must not have a competitive advantage over the private banks, that's the decisive point."
Other banks accused of benefiting from state capital injections are Bayerische Landesbank, Landesbank Schleswig-Holstein, Landesbank Berlin, and Norddeutsche Landesbank.
